title: The Windmill That Turns Wind Into Bread
blurb: A building with no engine and no fuel. It catches the wind, grinds grain into flour, and has been doing it for a thousand years.

blocks.prompt: The Mill With No Engine
blocks.text: A windmill has no engine. It has no fuel. It has one job: catch the wind and put it to work. Wind pushes on the four big sails. The sails turn. A long shaft inside the windmill turns too. The shaft turns a wheel, and the wheel turns a heavy stone. Under that stone is a second stone that never moves. Grain pours down between them. The stones grind the grain into flour. The miller lives with the wind. When the wind moves, he turns the whole top of the mill to face it. When the wind stops, the mill stops. So he waits.

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Runs on Weather
blocks.text: A windmill is a machine that runs on weather. Wind pushes against the sails. The sails are not flat boards. They are set at an angle, so passing air gives them a shove sideways, and the whole wheel begins to turn. That turning goes down a shaft, through a set of wooden gears, and into a millstone weighing more than a car. The stone spins just above a second stone that never moves at all. Grain trickles into a hole in the middle. It comes out at the edge as flour. The oldest windmills we know of were built in Persia, in what is now Iran, more than a thousand years ago. Some of them still stand in a village called Nashtifan, and on windy days some still turn. Windmills only work when the wind is blowing, and wind changes direction. So early European millers built the entire mill on a giant post and pushed the building around by hand until the sails faced the wind again. Imagine turning your whole house to catch a breeze.

blocks.prompt: Wind Is Sunlight in Disguise
blocks.text: Here is a strange fact to start with: wind is sunlight in disguise. The sun heats the ground unevenly. Warm air rises, cooler air slides in underneath to replace it, and that moving air is wind. So a windmill is really running on solar power, delivered the long way around. Getting that energy out is harder than it looks. Wind does not push a windmill so much as flow past it. The sails are angled and slightly twisted, like the wing of an airplane, so the air slipping over them pulls the wheel around rather than shoving it. A well-built mill turns in a breeze that a person would barely notice. The energy hidden in wind grows fast. Double the wind speed and you do not get twice the power, you get eight times as much. That is wonderful and dangerous at once. In a storm, a mill can spin faster than its own gears can survive. Millstones running with no grain between them throw sparks, and a mill full of flour dust burns like a torch. Millers climbed out onto the turning sails to roll up the canvas by hand and slow the machine down. In 1745, an English carpenter named Edmund Lee solved a different problem. He bolted a small wheel to the back of the mill, set sideways to the sails. When the wind shifted, that little wheel caught it, turned, and geared the whole cap around until the sails pointed into the wind again. The mill aimed itself. Nobody had to push anything. That is the quiet genius of the windmill. It has no engine and burns nothing at all, and for hundreds of years it was the most powerful machine most people would ever stand next to.

notes: Oldest known mills: Sistan, Persia, over 1,000 years ago

blocks.prompt: The Thousand-Year Machine
blocks.text: Every machine needs a source of power, and for most of human history there were only three: muscle, falling water, and moving air. Muscle tires. Water only flows where rivers run. Air is everywhere, free, and completely unreliable. The windmill is the long argument humans had with that last problem. The oldest windmills we can point to stood in Persia, in the Sistan region of what is now Iran, more than a thousand years ago. They looked nothing like the mills on a postcard. Their sails were mounted on a vertical shaft, like a revolving door, sheltered inside thick clay walls with a slot cut to let the wind strike one side only. In the village of Nashtifan, some of these mills still stand, and in the season of the fierce local winds, some still grind. Europe took a different path. By the twelfth century, English and French millers were building horizontal wheels, four great sails facing the weather, and immediately ran into the obvious flaw: wind will not hold still. Their answer was brute force. The post mill sat the entire building, machinery, grain, miller and all, on a single massive post, and when the wind swung around, someone leaned on a beam and pushed the whole thing until it faced the right way. Later builders got cleverer. The tower mill kept the body still and rotated only the cap. Then in 1745 Edmund Lee added the fantail, a small wheel mounted crosswise behind the sails. Any sideways wind spun it, and its gearing crept the cap back into the wind automatically. The mill had learned to aim itself, which is a form of thinking, done entirely with wood. The Dutch aimed windmills at a different enemy. Much of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and water does not drain uphill. So they pointed their mills at the water and lifted it out, mill after mill, each raising the water a little further, until a lake became a field. Nineteen of those mills still stand at Kinderdijk. The country was not just powered by wind. It was built by it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Nashtifan, Iran: vertical-axis mills roughly 1,000 years old
Post mill, 1100s: the whole building pivots on a post
Fantail, Edmund Lee, 1745: automatic wind-aiming
Betz limit, 1919: about 59 percent is the ceiling
Power scales with the cube of wind speed
A mill grinds, a turbine generates. Different machines

blocks.prompt: Forever Turning: How a Building Learned to Pay Attention
blocks.text: A windmill is a building that eats weather, and for roughly eight hundred years it was the most sophisticated machine an ordinary person would ever encounter. Start with the fuel, because the fuel is stranger than the machine. Wind is not really a thing in itself. The sun heats the Earth unevenly: bare ground faster than forest, land faster than ocean, the equator far faster than the poles. Warm air expands and rises, cooler air slides sideways to fill the gap, and that sideways slide is what we call wind. A windmill, then, is a solar machine. It just collects its sunlight secondhand, after the atmosphere has done the work of turning heat into motion. The oldest windmills we can document stood in the Sistan region of Persia, now eastern Iran, more than a thousand years ago. They bore no resemblance to the four-armed silhouette on a postcard. Their sails hung from a vertical shaft and spun like a revolving door, walled in on one side so the wind could only strike them from a single direction. A handful still stand at Nashtifan, and when the region's ferocious summer winds arrive, some of them still turn. Medieval Europe took a different design and inherited a different problem. A horizontal wheel with four sails out front catches far more wind, but only if it happens to be pointed at the wind. And wind does not hold still. The first European answer was gloriously crude: the post mill balanced the entire structure, gears, grindstones, grain and miller included, on one enormous vertical post, so a person with a lever could shove the whole building around to face the weather. The refinements that followed are where the story gets interesting. Tower mills fixed the body in place and turned only the cap. Then, in 1745, an English carpenter named Edmund Lee attached a small wheel to the rear of the cap, mounted at right angles to the main sails. When the wind blew straight into the sails, this fantail sat motionless in still air. The moment the wind shifted, it caught the crosswise breeze, spun, and through a train of gears rotated the cap until the sails faced the wind and the fantail stalled again. The machine sensed an error and corrected it. A wooden building had been taught to pay attention. The physics beneath all this is unforgiving. The power available in wind rises with the cube of its speed: double the wind and you get eight times the energy, which is why a mill that hums in a breeze can tear itself apart in a gale. Millers reefed the canvas by hand, climbing the turning sails to do it, and they feared fire above everything, because millstones grinding with no grain between them strike sparks into air thick with flour dust. Nor can any mill capture all the wind it meets. In 1919, Albert Betz proved why: to take every bit of energy out of moving air you would have to stop that air completely, and stopped air cannot get out of the way of the air behind it. The ceiling is about 59 percent. The Dutch pushed the machine hardest. Much of the Netherlands sits below sea level, and water will not drain uphill, so they set windmills to bail out an entire country, chains of them lifting water stage by stage until a lake became a field. Nineteen survive at Kinderdijk. Their millers even signaled with the sails, parking them in positions the next village could read: a brief pause, a long rest, a celebration, a death. Note the word we lost along the way. A windmill mills. The three-bladed towers on a modern ridgeline grind nothing, so they are turbines, not mills. They are the same idea, refined: the same twisted blade cheating the same reluctant air, chasing the same ceiling Betz drew in 1919.
